div.note: Liebermann's text is from D (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College 201, p. 43, after ‘Polity’ 25, in the same hand, c. 1060), the same manuscript as the modern edition. The heading is in red. Liebermann dates the text 1028–c. 1060 and places it at York. Clause number standardised from ‘Northu. Inscr.’.; AU: corrected against Rabin p. 302 / 303, October 2026 (was “Norðhymbra preosta lagu”, now “Norðhymbra preosta lagu (expanded letters in italics: Norðhymbra preosta lagu)”); W: corrected against Rabin p. 303, October 2026 (was “∅; Priests'”, now “The; Priests’”); F: corrected against Liebermann, Gesetze I (date in the running heads); Wormald, Making of English Law I, October 2026 (was “1028–c.1060; probably 1020–23 (Whitelock)”, now “1028–c.1060 (Liebermann); probably 1020–23 (Whitelock); after 1023 (Wormald)”); F: corrected against Liebermann, Gesetze I (date at the head of the text); Wormald, Making of English Law I; Whitelock, English Historical Documents I, October 2026 (was “1028–c.1060 (Liebermann); probably 1020–23 (Whitelock); after 1023 (Wormald)”, now “1028–c.1060 (Liebermann, I p. 380); probably 1020–23 (Whitelock, EHD p. 479); after 1023 (Wormald, MEL pp. 396–7)”); BQ: page of each of Liebermann’s texts and of his German, checked against Liebermann, Gesetze I (our double-read transcription), October 2026 (e.g. was “(empty)”, now “D 380; German 380”; 80 rows of Northu)

Der Gen. pl. Northymbra bezeichnet sowohl die Gegend wie die Laienbewohnerschaft, über welche die Priester Pfarrgewalt üben, nicht etwa die Nationalität der Priester.—Der Gen. preosta ist subjektiv: ‘durch sie [nicht bloss ‘für, über sie’] gegebenes Gesetz’; s. o. Einl. 10. Derselbe Begriff heisst u. 2, 3 preostlagu

The gen. pl. Northymbra denotes both the region and the lay population over which the priests exercise parochial authority, not, say, the nationality of the priests. — The gen. preosta is subjective: ‘law given by them’ [not merely ‘for them, about them’]; see above Introduction 10. The same concept is called preostlagu below 2, 3

Evidence relating to the north of England in the later Saxon period is scanty. This code shows us that heathen practices had still to be reckoned with, and it reveals a three-fold division of society for certain purposes, giving us a unique term to describe the lowest free class, for it seems to talk indiscriminately of a ceorl, a tunesmann “villager”, and a mysterious færbena. (see note on p. 474, below.) It reveals also the organisation of the priests of York into a community with common obligations and a common chest, the existence of the office of archdeacon in the northern province, and the toleration of the marriage of the clergy in this area. As Liebermann points out, the text falls into two parts which were probably originally distinct. Only chaps 1–45 constitute a priests’ law proper, and it may be that chaps 19–24, which do not, like the others, begin “If a priest…”, are a later accretion. The second part of the text, chaps 46 to the end, concerns itself with the behaviour of the laity in religious concerns, not with that of priests. Liebermann dates this second portion between 1028 and about 1060 (the date of the manuscript, C.C.C.C., MS. 201), but his earlier limit depends on his dating of the laws of Cnut, which this portion seems to use. This prevents him from assigning the document as a whole to the period when it was most likely to have come into being, the episcopate of Archbishop Wulfstan of York. As I have stated above (p. 454), I believe that Cnut’s laws belong to Wulfstan's lifetime, and there is nothing to prevent our assigning this code to his episcopate. The reasons for doing so are that the code survives only in a manuscript copied from a collection of his works and sources, which, though commonly assigned to Worcester, may be from York; and that all the known sources used in either part of the code are those written by Wulfstan, except for III Ethelred, a code for part of the Danelaw with which any archbishop of York would have to be familiar. It is also worth noting that a special point is made that a priest must not celebrate mass without wine. This is not specifically signalled out in the so-called Canons of Edgar which have been used tor this section, nor in the original text of Ælfric’s first pastoral letter for Wulfstan; but in the revision of this letter by Wulfstan, a clause is added: “And one is never to celebrate mass without wine.” As this version of the letter occurs in the same manuscript as the Priests’ Law, the clause in the latter could have been inserted by a later compiler; but surely it is more probable that it was a familiar abuse in this northern diocese in Wulfstan's time, and hence its addition to the letter, and its specific mention in the statutes drawn up for observance in his diocese. The connection with the so-called Canons of Edgar, which Jost has shown to be a work of Wulfstan’s, proves that the text is not earlier than his episcopate, and I see no necessity to put it later. The code is edited by Liebermann, I, 380–5; and with English translation by Thorpe, II, 290–303. [Her footnote 4: No. 53 in the 1955 edition] [Her footnote 5: see Whitelock, Franciplegius…studies in honor of F. P. Atagoun, jr, pp. 221–4. The connection between Worcester and York was broken after Wulfstan's time, except for 1040-1041, when Archbishop ÆIfric administered Worcester while Bishop Lifing was in disgrace, and for 1060–1062, when Ealdred held both sees.]
